column1: # External check: the Chakraborty et al. "Stop Clickbait" corpus (2016).
# 32,000 headlines, human-labeled, from OUTSIDE this project: 16,000
# clickbait headlines (BuzzFeed, Upworthy, ViralNova, Thatscoop, Scoopwhoop,
# ViralStories) and 16,000 ordinary ones (WikiNews, NYT, The Guardian, The
# Citation (required if this data is ever used in a publication):
# Chakraborty, Paranjape, Kakarla, Ganguly. "Stop Clickbait: Detecting and
# Preventing Clickbaits in Online News Media." ASONAM 2016.
# License: the source repository is MIT-licensed and asks that the paper above
# be cited. It states no separate license for the dataset. The headlines
# themselves were published by the outlets named above.
# The labels in harvested.tsv were reviewed by a language model, not a person: see
# docs/benchmark/review-process.md. That means they cannot be used to
# prove the rules work; they can only be checked against something truly
# independent. This corpus is that: labeled years ago, by different
# people, for a different project, with no knowledge of this app's rules.
# It does not use this project's nine-technique taxonomy: it's a plain
# yes/no "is this clickbait" call. Every "clickbait" row here is marked
# SUBTLE rather than PROMINENT because the source data has no strength
# rating, not because these headlines are mild. Treat "wrong strength" in
# rule-eval's output as meaningless noise on this file: read "wrongly
# flagged" and "missed" instead, those don't depend on the SUBTLE/PROMINENT
# choice. Also 2016-era headlines, mostly US entertainment sites, so it
# says nothing about UK tabloids or current outlets: see harvested.tsv for
